Networkingk8s 1.35

Packet Classification by Destination

A Pod sends to one address, so which machinery picks the packet up? The destination decides, because two stations stand between the Pod and the wire in a fixed order. The nat table owns the Service range and rewrites a Service address to a backend Pod address, then the route lookup sorts what it is handed into the Pod range, routed to the Node owning that slice, or into no cluster range at all, taken by the default route and masqueraded to the Node IP.

▶ Play the animation 5 steps, animated, best on a wide screen

How it works, step by step

  1. A packet leaves the Pod carrying one destination and naming no machinery. Two stations stand between it and the wire, in a fixed order, and only the second one is a routing decision. The nat table meets it first.

    Play from this step

  2. The destination 10.96.0.20:80 falls inside the Service range, so the nat table rewrites it to a backend Pod address, 10.244.2.7:8080 on Node-2. What leaves this station is no longer addressed to a Service.

    Play from this step

  3. The route lookup reads the rewritten address, which now sits inside the Pod range, and that range is cut into a slice per Node. So the packet goes to the Node owning 10.244.2.0/24, with no further rewrite.

    Play from this step

  4. A Pod addressing a Pod directly walks the same two stations in the same order. The nat table holds no rule for this address and passes it straight through, and the route lookup returns the very same verdict.

    Play from this step

  5. 1.1.1.1 falls in no cluster range, so the last resort takes it, the default route off the Node. Cluster traffic is excluded from MASQUERADE by default and this is not cluster traffic, so the source becomes the Node IP.

    Play from this step
